title: Module 8 — Tail
text:
Trailing edge holder
The wing root is driven by the gears and sweeps through the full 60° set in Module 5. The trailing edge is not driven. It is anchored to the tail tube, and that anchor is what makes the membrane twist as the wing sweeps. It sets the angle of attack the wing sees through the stroke. Move it and the wing behaves differently. So this part is a trim adjustment as much as it is a mount, which is why both its positions have to stay changeable after the robot is built.
This part is a design exercise. The requirements are fixed; the mechanism is not.



Table 1: What the trailing edge holder has to do





Requirement
Why




Rotates with the wing through the whole stroke
The root swings 34° up and 26° down. An anchor that cannot follow loads the membrane in the one direction it cannot take.


Adjustable longitudinally, along the tube
Fore/aft position sets wing twist. This is the trim actually reached for in Module 11.


Each Wing mounts can change laterally and longitudinally
Sets how far the anchor stands off the boom, and is how left and right are matched.


Wing comes off without dismantling anything
Wings get swapped, damaged and rebuilt. Nothing about this joint may be permanent.


Survives repeated wet cycling
To not fail at competition







Find a solution
Both flexible and rigid solutions are possible. For a rigid solution, the mount half is straightforward: a split collar that slides along the 5 mm tube and clamps with an M2 screw into a square half nut, per the house convention in Design notes. Sliding it gives the longitudinal adjustment, rotating it about the tube gives some of the lateral, and a slotted arm gives the rest.
The design must be justified against Table 1, and the choices defended.


Print it

3D-print the part with the material required.



Insert it on the tube
Slide the collar onto the tail tube and set it to the starting station. Measure from a fixed datum, write the number down, and set the second one to the same number.


Attach the wing
Connect each wing’s trailing edge to its holder.






WarningBoth sides must be set identically



Different longitudinal stations left and right means different twist left and right, which is a roll bias -the same failure mode as mismatched wings in Module 7, arriving by a different route and just as hard to trim out in Module 11.

Tail mounted, wings attached to tail.

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
section: Controlling the motor from a laptop
text:
Controlling the motor from a laptop
Next, install SimpleFOC Studio: SimpleFOCStudio. It is a desktop GUI that drives the same commander interface described below, so instead of typing commands into a serial monitor you get a form for every motor parameter, live plots of the monitored variables, and a button that dumps the tuned values back out as Arduino code.
Laptops can block the connection to the Seeeduino (over USB-C) if the Seeeduino is powered over 5V through the pin. If that happens, power needs to be disconnected. Two options are possible: either a UBS-C power isolation module or disconnecting the 5V line between ESC and Seeeduino.






WarningTorque control mode



Do not change the torque control mode in the GUI. It will display voltage mode but the ESC actually runs a newer estimated control mode.


Figure 1 shows the parts you will actually use: the parameter tree on the left, the live plot of target, velocity and angle in the middle, and a command line at the bottom for anything the form does not expose.






Figure 1: SimpleFOC Studio driving a motor. The tree on the left exposes every commander parameter as a form - motion control type, the four PID blocks, limits and sensor config - while the plot plays back target, velocity and angle as they change. Screen capture from the SimpleFOCStudio project.









NoteWhat the ESC code has to provide



Studio does not work against arbitrary firmware. The ESC code must register the motor with the commander (command.add('M', doMotor, "motor")), enable monitoring with motor.useMonitoring(Serial), and call both motor.monitor() and command.run() every loop. The command letter set in Studio’s device settings has to match the one in the sketch - M in our case.
On this robot the ESC’s own micro-USB serial is gone - those pins were repurposed for the encoder’s SPI3 bus in Module 3 - so the port Studio opens is the Seeeduino’s USB serial, and the Seeeduino has to pass what it receives through to the ESC on Serial1 (essentially it needs to act as a relay). Studio cannot reach the ESC on its own.

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
text:
Commanding and monitoring the ESC
This is a high-level summary of the SimpleFOC communication docs. The ESC is driven through the commander, a practical interface for setting and getting values (instructions). Ask the commander for available commands with ?. Commands available:







Command
Effect




M
Full motor configuration


F
Get the main loop frequency


L
Turn the onboard LED on and off (useful as a comms check)


T
Set the target value - rad, rad/s or N/m depending on control mode


S
Get current angle and velocity


W
Watchdog on/off. If no new target arrives for 1 s, target is set to zero. On by default


ME
Enable the driver. ME1 energises the phases, ME0 switches them off and the motor coasts


MC
Motion control type. MC0 torque, MC1 velocity, MC2 angle


MLC
Current limit, in amps



The M prefix is the motor command, and the letters after it walk down into its settings - MC is the motor’s control type, MLC the motor’s limit on current. That is why full configuration is just M on its own.
When it comes to commanding from the flight controlling direction, your code shouldn’t write these directly. Instead, you should create wrapper functions such as “current_limit(value)” etc…






WarningCareful when changing control mode



T means something different in each mode, position, velocity, or torque. Sending a velocity setpoint while in torque mode will do something unintended. BE VERY CAREFUL ABOUT THIS.



Tasks to do:

Change the motor command letter (towards the bottom in the interface) to M.
Commander responds to ? over serial from a laptop, L toggles the onboard LED.
The sensor returns a plausible angle through a full manual rotation.

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
text:
Tuning the cascaded controller
Figure 2 is the structure SimpleFOC implements. We need to tune it.






Figure 2: The cascaded controller. Desired angle enters on the left. The angle PID does not drive the motor - it produces a velocity target, which the velocity limit clamps. The velocity PID turns the velocity error into a target current, which the current limit clamps. Only the innermost torque/FOC stage touches the phases. Feedback runs the other way: the sensor returns angle, the derivative gives velocity, and both are low-pass filtered before use. Note the two rates — loopFOC() runs the torque stage, move() runs the two outer loops, and they are not the same frequency.



Each stage turns its own error into a setpoint for the stage inside it. That is the whole idea, and it is why the two clamps in the middle are not decoration: the velocity limit caps what the angle loop is allowed to ask for, and the current limit caps what the velocity loop is allowed to ask for.
Tune from the inside out. Work in this order, and do not move outwards until the loop you are on behaves:

Torque first, in torque mode (MC0). Command a current and check the motor takes it smoothly, without whine or oscillation.
Velocity next (MC1), once torque is solid. Proportional gain first, then integral. Watch the low-pass filter on the velocity feedback while you do: heavy filtering looks like it is cleaning up noise, but the lag it adds is what makes the loop hunt.
Angle last (MC2). Usually proportional gain alone is enough, because the velocity loop underneath is already doing the work.

The order is not a convention, it is a dependency. An outer loop tuned against a sloppy inner loop is partly compensating for the inner loop’s error, so its gains encode that error - and they stop being valid the moment you go back and fix the inner loop.
These four PID blocks are exactly what SimpleFOC Studio exposes in its parameter tree (Figure 1). That is the practical argument for having installed it: you can change a gain and watch the step response without reflashing between attempts.
SimpleFOC documents each stage separately: torque control, the velocity loop, the angle loop, and cascaded position control for the structure in Figure 2 as a whole. The exact forms being tuned are in the PID implementation and the low-pass filter.

Record how it responds to a step change:
Do these in Studio. For each one, capture the step response and write down the gains that produced it. A screenshot without its gains is not a result: nobody can reproduce it.
Two things to set before the first capture.

Turn the watchdog off for the duration (W0). It is on by default and zeroes the target after 1 s without a new one, so it will pull your step back down in the middle of the capture and look like a controller fault.
Plot the variable the loop actually controls - current in torque mode, velocity in velocity mode, angle in position mode - and leave Target enabled in all three so the step is visible.


Torque mode (MC0). Set the velocity limit to 200 rad/s, then block the output with your hand or a piece of tape before commanding any current - in torque mode nothing limits speed, so an unblocked motor just accelerates until friction stops it. Set the current limit with MLC, starting around 1 A, and step the target.
Velocity mode (MC1). Step from standstill to 400 rad/s and capture the response. Note that this is motor speed, not the flapping frequency of the final system. Mount a small flag (piece of tape) on the output so rotation is visible and countable.
Position mode (MC2). Step from 0 to 144 rad and back to 0 - about a full flap cycle after reduction - and capture the response.

Report rise time, overshoot and any steady-state error read off the plot.






WarningA blocked motor turns every amp into heat



With the output held there is no back-EMF and no mechanical work, so all the electrical power goes into the windings. Apply the torque step in bursts of a few seconds and let the motor cool between attempts if needed.

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
section: Why we use an ESC that we reprogram
text:
Why we use an ESC that we reprogram

Why low speed is the hard part
Regular drone ESCs start losing synchronisation at low speed, which is exactly the regime used for water propulsion. That is the reason this course uses an FOC ESC rather than a hobby unit - see Design notes.


Why high speed is the hard part (going beyond 600 rad/s)
Two issues limit speed: the micro-controller loop rate, and delays from the rotation sensor. Using SPI at 10 MHz and an AS5047P sensor rated for 28kRPM speeds are the required hardware changes that improves on delay. But at very high speeds, sensor lag still becomes the binding constraint, and shows up as high current draw and noise. We need to update the sensor electrical angle offset as a function of speed. Compensating sensor lag as speed increases is necessary to go above 600 rad/s without wasting current. This is automated by ramping through the speeds and minimising phase current. This SimpleFOC forum thread is useful on the topic.






NoteCheckpoint



Continuous rotation at 1 Hz, position hold against a hand disturbance, and a recorded loop frequency from F. The robot should be tuned, operating in various modes and can be commanded from the flight controller

title: Module 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
The motor - AS2303 KV1500
The AS2303 is a brushless outrunner. Read Brushless motors first.

We use the AS2303 KV1500 motor throughout the course. Its propeller horn cannot be separated from the bell.

What the KV rating means
KV is the motor’s velocity constant, quoted in rpm per volt. It says how fast the rotor spins per volt applied, with no load on the shaft:
\[\omega_0 = k_V \, U \tag{1}\]
The constant is not a marketing number - it falls out of the motor’s physics. As the rotor turns, its magnets sweep past the windings and induce a voltage that opposes the supply (the back-EMF):
\[U_\text{emf} = \frac{\omega}{k_V} \tag{2}\]
The supply voltage splits between this back-EMF and the ohmic drop across the winding resistance \(R\), so \(U = U_\text{emf} + R\,I\) and the speed under load becomes
\[\omega = k_V \left( U - R\,I \right) \tag{3}\]
which is why Equation 1 only holds at \(I \approx 0\). Draw current and the motor slows down.
A high-KV motor spins fast but gives little torque per amp; a low-KV motor of the same size and mass does the opposite. Both cannot be had at once - the choice is where to sit on that trade-off, and then to recover the missing torque with a reduction.


What this means for our robot
With \(k_V = 1500\) rpm/V and a 4S LiPo at its 14.8 V nominal voltage:
\[\omega_0 = 1500 \times 14.8 = 22\,200 \ \text{rpm}
\qquad
k_T = \frac{9.55}{1500} = 6.4 \ \text{mN·m/A}\]
6.4 mN·m/A is very little torque, too little to drive the wings directly, which is exactly why the 23.04:1 Faulhaber gearbox is there. It multiplies torque by 23.04 and divides speed by the same factor. One revolution of the gearbox output is one full flapping cycle, so
\[f_\text{flap} = \frac{\omega}{60 \, r}
= \frac{22\,200}{60 \times 23.04} = 16.1 \ \text{Hz} \tag{4}\]
at no load. Under real aerodynamic and hydrodynamic loading the drive tops out near 15 200 rpm, i.e. about 11 Hz of flapping, the figure that reappears in Module 4.

title: Module 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
Motor shaft
To pair the motor with the gearbox, the stock shaft of the brushless motor is replaced by a custom one. What is left to do is the disassembly and the press fit, which is still a delicate operation: the motor’s structure is mostly aluminium and quite thin, for weight savings.

Remove the circlip on the shaft with the special pliers. Don’t lose it, nor the brass ring.
Separate the rotor from the stator delicately, by hand.
Press the stock shaft out of the rotor bell.






WarningNever load the bell radially



Press the shaft out very carefully, making sure to never apply forces radially on the bell. Use the manual press with appropriate support below the bell to avoid deforming the dome shape. Do not squeeze the bell with a vice, or even by hand.


Press the new shaft into the bell, making sure not to press on the dome-shaped part of the bell without appropriate support underneath. It is a tight fit on the bell and a clearance fit through the bearings.







Figure 1: Motor shaft dimensions

title: Module 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
Sensor magnet
The AS5047P encoder wired up in Module 3 does not touch the shaft. It reads the direction of the magnetic field from a small magnet rotating in front of it, so the magnet has to go on the motor.
Use a 6 × 2.5 mm diametrically magnetised disc magnet. Diametrically magnetised is the part that matters: the poles are across the diameter, not through the thickness, so the field seen by the sensor sweeps through a full rotation as the shaft turns. An ordinary axially magnetised disc of identical size presents the same pole to the sensor all the way round and gives no angle at all.

Drop the magnet into its recess in the 3D-printed bracket. It should sit flat, fully seated, with no rocking.
Centre it on the axis of rotation. The bracket locates it, but check. Keep the magnet concentric with the shaft to within 0.5 mm.
Bond it with a single drop of superglue. One drop is enough.
Turn the assembly through a full revolution by hand and watch the magnet. Any visible wobble means it is off-centre or not seated.







WarningOff-centre magnets are hard to diagnose later



An eccentric magnet may still produces a perfectly plausible angle reading at times.

Mounting the motor
With the shaft and the magnet done, the motor goes onto the robot plate. This happens in two stages: motor to bracket, then bracket to plate.

Fix the motor to the vertical 3D-printed nylon bracket using four screws M2x5 mm through the mounting holes in the motor base. Don’t over tighten. Check that the rotor still turns freely by hand. Nylon is compliant, and overtightening can pull the bracket out of flat enough to preload the bearings. A motor that spun freely on the bench and feels stiff once bolted down needs the screws backed off and retightened more gently.
Insert square half-nuts in the slots in the motor bracket. Mount the bracket to the bottom fuselage plate. Before tightening, check the orientation: the shaft and sun gear must point towards the front of the robot.

title: The G431 ESC board
text: Background on the B-G431B-ESC1, the board you rework and flash in Module 3. What is on it, how it turns a DC battery into three moving phases, what it can drive, and why it arrives in two pieces.

title: The G431 ESC board
text:
What it is
ST sells this as a Discovery kit: a reference design showing what their STM32G431 can do in a motor-control role, in the physical form of a drone ESC. That origin explains most of its oddities. A hobby ESC exposes a signal wire and two power leads because that is all a flight controller needs; this board brings out a CAN bus, a potentiometer input, a hall-sensor connector and a debug header, because its job is to demonstrate everything the chip supports.
For us the consequence is good and bad in equal measure. Good: the silicon is open, we can run our own firmware (SimpleFOC) and we get real current sensing. Bad: several connectors are wired for uses we do not want, which is why Module 3 spends its time repurposing them.

The MCU is the interesting choice. FOC recomputes the field orientation every control loop, and each iteration costs a handful of trigonometric evaluations (see How SimpleFOC works). At 170 MHz with hardware floating point that fits comfortably inside a 10 kHz loop. A hobby ESC’s 8-bit microcontroller could not do this arithmetic in the time available, which is precisely why hobby ESCs use the cruder back-EMF scheme instead.

title: The G431 ESC board
section: How the three phases are generated
text:
How the three phases are generated
The battery supplies one DC voltage. The motor needs three voltages that vary smoothly and stay 120° apart. The bridge between the two is built from three identical circuits.
One half-bridge per phase. Each phase output connects to two MOSFETs in series across the battery: a high-side switch to the positive rail and a low-side switch to ground. Closing the high side pulls that phase to battery voltage; closing the low side pulls it to zero. Three phases, three pairs, six transistors — the six packages in Figure 1.
PWM makes the intermediate values. A switch is either on or off, so a half-bridge can only output the full rail or nothing. Switching between them tens of thousands of times a second and varying the fraction of time spent high produces any average voltage in between. 50% duty gives half the rail. The motor’s own winding inductance does the smoothing: it resists rapid current changes, so it responds to the average and largely ignores the switching.
Three of them, offset, make a rotating field. Drive the three duty cycles as sinusoids 120° apart and the three phase voltages produce a magnetic field that sweeps steadily around the stator. Advance the sinusoids faster and the field rotates faster. This is what driver.setPwm(Ua, Ub, Uc) at the bottom of SimpleFOC’s inner loop is ultimately setting.






WarningBoth switches in a pair must never be on together



High and low side closed at once is a direct short across the battery through two transistors — called shoot-through, and it destroys the pair in microseconds. The hardware inserts a dead time: a brief interval where both are off during every transition. It is handled by the gate drivers and the MCU’s timer, so you will not code it, but it is why the two switches of a pair are never driven by a single signal.


Current sensing closes the loop. A small-value shunt resistor sits in each phase’s low-side return path. The voltage across it is proportional to the current through that phase; the MCU amplifies and samples it. Three shunts mean all three phase currents are visible, which is what makes true FOC current control possible rather than voltage-mode approximation. Without this measurement you can ask for a torque; with it you can regulate one.

Two cautions about that 40 A. It is a peak figure, and it assumes forced air — a fan, or a drone’s propwash. Our robot has neither, and it spends much of its life underwater with the board sealed inside potting compound (Module 10), so heat leaves slowly and only by conduction. Treat 40 A as a number describing the silicon, not a budget you may spend.
In practice this is not the binding constraint. The wing motor draws far less than the board can supply, so the limits you will actually meet are the motor’s own thermal limit and sensor lag, not the ESC’s. The relevant discussion is in Brushless motors and Module 4.

title: The G431 ESC board
text:
Why there is a daughterboard
The small board at the end is a complete ST-LINK/V2-1 programmer and debug probe. It is separated from the power board by a line of perforations and is meant to be snapped off.
That design makes sense for ST’s intended user: develop with the programmer attached, then break it away so the flight-ready ESC is smaller and lighter, and reuse the same programmer on the next board. It carries two things:

SWD — the debug and programming interface, used to flash the MCU
A virtual COM port — a USB serial bridge onto one of the MCU’s UARTs







ImportantDo not snap it off



Once separated, reprogramming needs an external programmer wired to the SWD pads by hand. We keep it attached for the whole course. This is also why the board is larger than a hobby ESC of equivalent power — roughly half of what you are holding is the programmer.


The virtual COM port is where Module 3 runs into trouble. Out of the box it is wired to the MCU’s USART2, on pins that the board also uses for the hall-sensor connector. Those same pins are the SPI3 bus we need for the AS5047P encoder, and an encoder is not optional for FOC. So the pins go to the encoder, USART2 stops being reachable over USB, and serial has to be re-routed — either onto USART1 by rework, or off-board entirely to the Seeeduino. Flashing is unaffected throughout, because SWD runs on different pins.

title: Brushless motors
text: Background for Module 2.

title: Brushless motors
section: Start with the brushed DC motor
text:
Start with the brushed DC motor
Every result you need for a brushless motor is easier to see in a brushed one first, because the two obey the same electrical physics. The difference is how the windings get switched, not what the machine does once they are.
A DC motor is described by two constants and one resistance. Spinning the rotor induces a back-EMF proportional to speed, and passing current through the windings produces torque proportional to current:
\[U_\text{emf} = \frac{\omega}{k_V} \qquad\qquad \tau = k_T \, I \tag{1}\]
These are the same \(k_V\) and \(k_T\) derived in Module 2 — inverses of each other, not independent choices. The supply voltage splits between the back-EMF and the ohmic drop across the winding resistance \(R\):
\[U = \frac{\omega}{k_V} + R \, I \tag{2}\]
Substitute \(I = \tau / k_T\) and rearrange for torque, and the whole behaviour of the motor falls out as a straight line:
\[\tau = k_T \frac{U}{R} - \frac{k_T}{k_V R}\,\omega \tag{3}\]

Reading the torque-speed line
That line is the motor’s entire steady-state character, and it is fixed by the applied voltage. Two points define it:

Stall torque \(\tau_\text{stall} = k_T U / R\), at \(\omega = 0\). The rotor is held still, there is no back-EMF, and the only thing limiting current is the winding resistance. This is the largest torque the motor can produce and also the fastest way to destroy it - see Thermal limits.
No-load speed \(\omega_0 = k_V U\), at \(\tau = 0\). The rotor spins fast enough that the back-EMF nearly cancels the supply, so almost no current flows.

Everything the motor can do at that voltage lies on the line between them. Mechanical power is \(P = \tau \omega\), the product of a falling line and a rising one, so it is a parabola peaking at half the no-load speed with half the stall torque. Efficiency peaks somewhere else entirely — much closer to \(\omega_0\), because the copper loss that dominates at low speed scales with \(I^2\) while the useful output only scales with \(I\).









NoteThe useful consequence



Raising the voltage shifts the line outwards without changing its slope: more speed and more torque, same trade-off between them. That is why speed control is voltage control, and why a “faster” motor at fixed voltage is a lower-torque one.

title: Brushless motors
section: What changes with a brushless motor
text:
What changes with a brushless motor
In a brushed motor the commutator and brushes are a mechanical switch riding on the rotor: they physically reconnect the windings as it turns, so the current always flows in whichever coil is best placed to produce torque. It works without any electronics at all, and it wears out, arcs, and limits how fast the motor can safely spin.
A BLDC motor deletes that switch. The permanent magnets go on the rotor, the windings stay on the stator in three phases, and an external controller decides which phases to energise based on where the rotor currently is. The motor becomes inseparable from its driver — this is why Module 3 exists, and why the rotor position measurement matters so much.
What this does not change is Equation 3. The torque and speed constants have the same meaning, the line has the same shape, and you size the motor the same way. What changes is that the line is no longer the whole story:









Brushed
Brushless




Commutation
Mechanical, self-acting
Electronic, needs rotor position


Torque–speed line
The real limit
The ideal limit, then clipped by the driver


Wear
Brushes are consumable
Bearings only


Speed ceiling
Brush arcing and bounce
Commutation rate and sensor lag


Torque ripple
Smoothed by many commutator segments
Depends on drive scheme (trapezoidal vs FOC)




The envelope, not the line
The straight line assumes the supply can deliver whatever current the equations ask for. It cannot. At stall, Equation 2 gives \(I = U/R\), and with the sub-ohm winding resistance of a small outrunner that is a number in the hundreds of amps — far beyond both the ESC and the motor itself.
So the driver enforces a current limit, and because \(\tau = k_T I\) that is directly a torque limit. The usable region becomes:

a constant-torque region at low speed, flat at whatever current limit you set, because the ESC is holding current rather than letting the line dictate it;
a corner speed where the back-EMF has risen enough that the supply can no longer push that current;
above it, the original Equation 3 line, falling to \(\omega_0\).

The flat part is not physics, it is a decision. On our robot it is the decision that keeps the motor alive at the low speeds used for swimming, where the torque–speed line alone would happily draw enough current to cook the windings.

title: Brushless motors
text:
Thermal limits
Nothing in Equation 3 knows about heat, which is why the equations cheerfully predict operating points that will destroy the motor in seconds.
Almost all the loss you care about is copper loss in the windings:
\[P_\text{copper} = I^2 R \tag{4}\]
The square is what makes this the binding constraint. Doubling the torque doubles the current and quadruples the heating. A motor comfortable at its rated current will not survive twice that for long, even though the torque equation says it is only a factor of two.
Three practical consequences:

Stall is the worst case, not the best. At \(\omega = 0\) there is maximum current and no rotation, so no airflow and no useful output — all the input power becomes heat in the windings. A motor held at stall can burn out without the shaft moving at all.
Continuous and peak ratings are different numbers. A peak rating assumes seconds; a continuous rating assumes thermal equilibrium. Flapping is a reciprocating load, so the current is far from constant — what matters for heating is the RMS current over the cycle, not the peak you see on the bench supply.
Iron losses grow with speed. Hysteresis and eddy-current losses in the stator scale with electrical frequency, so at the 1700 rad/s discussed in Module 4 the copper is no longer the only thing getting warm.










WarningHeat is cumulative and invisible



Current is the only symptom you can see, and it appears instantly, while the temperature it causes lags behind by tens of seconds. A run that looks fine on the ammeter can still be depositing heat faster than the motor sheds it. When tuning in Module 4, stop and touch the motor.

title: Brushless motors
text:
Why an outrunner
Brushless motors come in two arrangements. An inrunner spins a magnet rotor inside a stationary stator, the familiar shape from a drill. An outrunner inverts it: the stator sits still in the middle and the magnets are carried on a bell that rotates around the outside. Ours is an outrunner — it is the bell you machine and press the shaft into in Module 2.






Figure 1: An outrunner seen from the back. The copper windings are the stator and do not move; the dark magnet segments around the rim are carried on the rotating bell. Note how far out the magnets sit — that radius is the lever arm in Equation 5, and it is the whole reason for this arrangement. Note also that the heat is generated in the middle, wrapped inside the part that spins.



The reason is torque. Torque is force times radius, and in an outrunner the magnets sit at the largest radius the motor’s diameter allows, rather than the smallest:
\[\tau = F \times r \tag{5}\]
The same tangential force from the same windings acts on a longer lever arm. It also leaves room for more magnet poles around the circumference. Together these raise \(k_T\) for a motor of the same mass, which by Equation 1 means a lower KV — more torque per amp, less speed per volt.
That is the right trade for us. The wings need torque at low speed, through a gearbox that is already multiplying by 23.04:1, and the alternative is either a larger reduction or more current for the same result. Two secondary properties help as well:

Rotor inertia. The rotating mass is at a large radius, so the bell has significant inertia and acts as a flywheel. Against a reciprocating flapping load that smooths the speed variation over a cycle. It also means the motor cannot change speed quickly, which is a real cost during transients.
Something to attach to. The bell is a large-diameter rotating surface, which is what makes the shaft press-fit in Module 2 mechanically sensible in the first place.

The costs are real: outrunners spin more slowly for a given voltage, the exposed rotating bell is a hazard and an ingress path, and cooling is worse because the heat-producing stator is wrapped inside the rotor rather than mounted against the case. The last point ties directly back to Thermal limits — an outrunner’s stator sheds heat mainly through its mount, which on our robot is a 3D-printed plate.

title: How SimpleFOC works
text: The firmware in FAAV-G431-ESC is a SimpleFOC application. This page is what you need to read that firmware and change it with confidence: what the library computes, in what order, and where your settings enter. It is background for Module 3 and Module 4, not a procedure.

title: How SimpleFOC works
text:
The problem it solves
A brushless motor has three windings and no brushes, so nothing decides on its own which winding should be energised. Something has to look at where the rotor is and energise the windings to put the stator’s magnetic field about 90° ahead of the rotor’s magnets, the orientation that produces the most torque per amp. Do that continuously and the motor behaves like a brushed DC motor: torque proportional to current, no commutator to wear out. That is Field-Oriented Control, and it is why Module 2’s \(\tau = k_T I\) is usable at all.
The awkward part is that “90° ahead” is a statement about a rotating frame, while the three phase currents live in a stationary one. FOC is mostly the bookkeeping that moves between the two.

title: How SimpleFOC works
section: Three objects, and what links them
text:
Three objects, and what links them
The SimpleFOC architecture is built around three objects, each wrapping one piece of hardware:



Object
Wraps
Our hardware




MagneticSensorSPI
The angle sensor
AS5047P on SPI3


BLDCDriver6PWM
The inverter
Six MOSFETs on the G431


BLDCMotor
The control maths
—



BLDCMotor owns the algorithm and is told about the other two with linkSensor() and linkDriver(). Nothing else connects them, which is why a missing link call produces a motor that initialises cleanly and then does nothing sensible.

title: How SimpleFOC works
text:
The two loops
Every iteration runs two nested controllers, and keeping them straight is most of understanding the library:

motor.loopFOC() — the inner loop. Reads the angle, works out where the field should point, and sets the PWM duty cycles. It runs as fast as you can call it (above 10 kHz), and its rate is the loop frequency you read back with the commander’s F command.
motor.move(target) — the outer loop. Turns your setpoint (a position, a speed, or a torque) into the q-axis demand the inner loop chases.

The inner loop is where speed matters; the outer loop is where tuning matters.






WarningBoth must be called every iteration



loopFOC() without move() holds whatever demand it last had. move() without loopFOC() updates a number nothing acts on. Anything blocking in loop() - a delay(), a slow print - drops the inner-loop rate and shows up as a motor that runs rough at speed.

title: How SimpleFOC works
section: What the inner loop actually computes

title: How SimpleFOC works
How SimpleFOC works
section: Alignment, and why the motor twitches at power-on
text:
Alignment, and why the motor twitches at power-on
motor.initFOC() performs the one calibration FOC cannot do without. The sensor reports some absolute angle, but nothing tells it how that number relates to the motor’s magnetic poles - that depends on how the magnet was glued on and how the phase wires happened to be soldered. So initFOC() drives a known field, watches which way the rotor moves and where it settles, and stores two things:

zero_electric_angle - the offset between sensor zero and electrical zero
sensor direction - whether the sensor counts up or down relative to the motor’s positive rotation

That is the twitch you see at every power-on. If it is skipped or wrong, the field is placed at the wrong angle and the motor draws current while producing little torque, or runs away.






NoteWhy the UVW order does not matter



Module 3 says you can solder the phase wires in any order. Swapping two phases reverses the motor’s direction, and initFOC() measures direction rather than assuming it - so the calibration simply comes out with the other sign. The cost of getting it “wrong” is a stored constant, not a rework.

title: How SimpleFOC works
How SimpleFOC works

Robot operation in one paragraph
One 4S battery (16.8 V max) feeds an custom ESC that steps VBAT down to 5 V to power the flight controller and the encoder. The flight controller commands the ESC over serial. The ESC drives a brushless motor through a 23.04:1 gearbox, and a crank–linkage converts that rotation into undulation motion.

title: Module 3 — Motor driver, sensor and serial connection
text:
Electronic Speed Controller
The B-G431B-ESC1 is ST’s reference three-phase motor driver: a complete ESC on one small board, sold as an evaluation kit. It contains: - An STM32G431 microcontroller. A 170 MHz Cortex-M4 with hardware floating point. Motor control recomputes the field orientation every control loop. This MCU is the reason we can. - A three-phase inverter. Six power MOSFETs drive the three motor phases. - A detachable ST-Link programmer (the daughterboard). The small daughter board is how we program the MCU over USB, and it also carries a serial port back to the laptop. When snapped-off, the MCU cannot be reprogramed without physically resoldering it.
It also brings out many input/outputs (for exampleJ8), a CAN transceiver and a potentiometer input, none of which we use as intended. In this build J8 gets repurposed for serial, and the encoder arrives on SPI instead. Both of those reworks are below. The board is rated well above what the wing motor draws (40A), so current is not the constraint here. Get familiar with every component on the board, how six MOSFETs turn one DC rail into three rotating phases, what current it can actually deliver, and why the programmer is a separate snap-off board under The G431 ESC board.

text:
Flight controller microcontroller
We will use a Seeeduino XIAO nRF52840 Sense to send commands to the ESC and record information from the ESC. Why?

It is small and light. 21 × 17.5 mm and 2.4 g. On a robot that has to move, every gram saved matters.
It has wireless communication out of the box. The nRF52840 is a Bluetooth Low Energy chip and a microcontroller. Once the robot is sealed in Module 10 BLE becomes the only way commands to interact with the robot during operation, which is exactly how a run is retrieved in Module 11.
It has somewhere to put the data. 256 kB of RAM and 1 MB of flash on the chip itself are the two logging destinations used during wet testing. No SD card, no extra memory chip, nothing else to waterproof.
Onboard IMU to log the attitude of the robot without additional components.
It costs 20$. In case a failure, it can be replaced.

It programs from the Arduino IDE like any other Arduino board, but we highly recommend using Visual Studio Code + PlatformIO. The reason for PlatformIO is that it handles multiple-file projects much better, allows git versioning and handles libraries better. It also provides a more performant editor.






Figure 4: The Seeeduino XIAO nRF52840. TX and RX are the two pads at the bottom corners — those are the ones to solder to, and they cross over to the ESC’s RX and TX respectively. The board is 21 × 17.5 mm, which is why it can ride on the robot at all.




Solder the Seeeduino and the ESC’s Serial1: TX, RX and GND lines. For that, use the 6x30AWG wire ribbon, spliced (only need 4 lines). In Serial communication, TX and RX are crossed, each board’s transmit line goes to the other’s receive line, as drawn in the wiring diagram in Module 3. GND is not optional: without a shared reference the two boards have no agreed voltage for what counts as a high or low bit.
Verify that you can command the LED of the seeeduino on and off first. This requires Visual Studio Code and the PlatformIO plugin installed. Leave the ESC unpowered for now.
Load the barebone Arduino sketch onto the Seeeduino, modify it if needed, see Software for the repository.
Load the default ESC code onto the ESC via its daughterboard (via micro-usb).
Prepare the USB-C 15V power source. We are using a USB-C power delivery cable to power the robot on the bench. A PD supply does not simply hand over whatever voltage you want. It advertises a fixed menu, and the sink has to negotiate for one of them, which is why we use a PD trigger cable or board is needed to pin it at 15 V. Table 1 is the power available.

title: Module 3 — Motor driver, sensor and serial connection
text:
Encoder (or Angular sensor)

First, why does the motor need an encoder?
Field-Oriented Control works by holding the stator’s magnetic field roughly 90° ahead of the rotor’s magnets, which is the orientation that produces the most torque per amp. To place the field there, the controller has to know where the rotor is right now.
Ordinary drone ESCs infer this from back-EMF, i.e the voltage the spinning rotor induces in the phase that is not currently being driven (?@eq-bemf in Module 2). That voltage is proportional to speed, so as the motor slows the signal sinks into the noise and the estimate falls apart. This causes loss of synchronisation at low speed described in Design notes. The AS5047P removes the guess. It measures the field of the magnet bonded to the shaft end and reports the absolute angle - valid at standstill just as much as at 15 000 rpm, and correct immediately at power-on with no homing move.


What SPI is, and why we run it at 10 MHz
We will use an AS5047P encoder. The AS5047P reports angle over SPI, a four-wire synchronous bus: the controller drives the clock (SCLK), data goes out on MOSI and comes back on MISO, and CS selects the chip. Transfer speed is limited only by how fast the two ends can shift bits. We use SPI because it offers 10 MHz communication. The reason speed matters is that the angle has to be re-read every single control loop, and a stale angle is bad: the controller ends up placing the stator field where the rotor was, not where it is. That error shows up as wasted current and audible noise. The same 10 MHz clock is why the wiring has to stay short, see below.


Wire it to the board
There is no SPI link exposed directly on the ESC board. The solution is to use the SPI3 bus, exposed through a few hardware modifications and matching software changes. Figure 1 shows the four signals in context, including the MOSI tap on R14.






WarningThe micro-USB serial link is lost



Serial2, used by the daughterboard for serial communication will not work anymore as we are using those pins for SPI3 for the encoder instead. Flashing the ESC still works (programming runs over SWD, on different pins) but every command and every value read back now has to pass through serial1 (external TX/RX).


The encoder needs power as well as the four bus signals - six wires in total. Replace the default cable and use the 6x30AWG wire ribbon instead. This is small work! Sit down, use a clean soldering iron, take your time and make sure you have lots of light.
Check the R14 connection under the microscope. Use a drop of glue to fix the cable onto the board






Figure 5: The MOSI tap on R14 under the microscope. The wire lands on the outward side of the resistor, and the bead of clear glue over the joint is to help with accidental pulls on the cable.

text:
Reduction
The motor is connected via a custom shaft to a gearbox with a 23.04:1 reduction by Faulhaber.2 Both parts are held in place by 3D-printed plates. The output shaft of the gearbox has its own bearing on the inside of the gearbox, and is also supported mid-way on the shaft by a 4×8 mm flanged bearing. This leaves 5 mm of shaft length free for the crank to be mounted on. A flat on the shaft helps lock the rotation of the M3 screw extending through the crank.






Motor shaft







Faulhaber gearbox





First, we need to press + glue our sun gear is already pressed onto the motor shaft from Module 2.
Next, we need to install the gearbox to the motor and fixing the pair to the plates.

Slide the gearbox onto the motor shaft so the sun gear engages the planets. It should seat with light hand pressure, if it resists, back off and check the sun gear is square on the shaft rather than forcing it.
Fix the blue part of the gearbox: the custom screws that come with the gearbox on one side, and M2.5×10 screws on the other.
Check the output turns freely by hand through a full revolution before applying power.
Close the gearbox: the silver part threads onto the blue part. Don’t tighten it.
Attach the second vertical bracket to the silver part of the gearbox with 3 × M2.5 screws.
Secure that bracket to the bottom fuselage plate with 3 × M2 screws. The motor bracket from Module 2 is already on the same plate, so between them the two brackets set the alignment of the whole drivetrain. Check the output still turns freely once both are bolted down.

text:
Example and tips for building the wing
The whole wing is built over the printed pattern, working from the leading edge outwards. Everything is cut oversize and trimmed to the outline at the very end - margin is easy to remove and impossible to add back.

Decide on the shape and print the pattern on paper. Print it 1:1 - check the scale before cutting anything, by measuring a known dimension on the printout against a rule. Printer drivers scale to fit by default, and a pattern that came out at 97% quietly discards the geometry chosen in Module 6.
Cut two membranes with a 3 cm margin all round the pattern. Use the ripstop nylon listed in Parts.
Bond the leading edge. Lay a strip of 3M tape along the leading-edge region of the membrane, press the leading-edge rod down onto the tape, and wrap the membrane around the rod. This joint carries the highest load of any on the wing — everything downstream pulls against it.
Lay out the carbon strips. Cut each to approximate length plus 3 cm, position them on the membrane over the pattern, and bond them with superglue.
Stitch the strips down, at minimum at every intersection point and at the extremities. Superglue alone will peel off the membrane under repeated flapping; the stitches are what keep the skeleton attached once the glue starts to fail.
Trim the excess beyond the outline with a blade, cutting on the mat.







Strips laid out and bonded over the template







Trimming the membrane to the outline





Repeat for the second wing, and remember that it is flipped.

title: Module 11 — Wet testing
text:
The tank
Testing happens in the AURA Lab tank. The gantry along the near rail and the cameras overhead are part of the measurement setup, not scenery — the ceiling cameras are what track the robot for the cost-of-transport number below.






Figure 1: The AURA Lab tank. The rail and gantry run the length of the near side; the tracking cameras are mounted overhead.









WarningTank rules (repeat)



Nobody gets in the tank. Not to retrieve a robot, not to reposition it, not for a moment. Use the poles to fish the robot back to the edge.
Keep water off the floor. Water on the floor sets off an alarm, which ends the session for everyone. Lift the robot out over the tank and let it drain there rather than carrying it dripping, and keep towels to hand for what gets past. Dry the floor immediately if it happens.

title: Module 11 — Wet testing
text:
What to log
Every run should record, at minimum:

Power consumption — the numerator of cost of transport
IMU data — attitude and acceleration through the run
Flapping frequency — the input being varied

Since underwater we lose wireless communication, the data needs to be recorded and streamed back wirelessly after the run. There are two places to record data on the flight controller, and the choice matters more than it looks:









RAM
Flash




Survives power loss
No
Yes


Speed
Fast, no wear
Slower, finite write cycles


Use it for
The normal case
Runs that cannot afford to be repeated



The normal workflow is log to RAM during the run, then broadcast over BLE once the robot is out of the water. Nothing has to be opened and nothing has to be plugged in, which is the whole point: the board is potted from Module 10 and there is no connector to reach.






WarningRAM is lost the moment power goes



A brownout, a watchdog reset, or an accidental disconnect takes the whole run with it. Broadcast the data before changing the battery, not after - and if a run is expensive to repeat, write it to flash instead.

title: Module 11 — Wet testing
text:
Housing
Design and 3D-print an exterior housing to ensure neutral buoyancy as needed. Foam can also be used.

title: Module 11 — Wet testing
text:
Trim
Two independent adjustments, both mechanical. Change one at a time with a run between them, otherwise there is no telling which one did what.

Wing trim
Wing trim is adjusted at the trailing edge.






ImportantTo be completed by the instructor



The trailing-edge trim part itself is not designed yet — decide what it is, how it mounts, and what range of adjustment it gives. Until then this step cannot be written as a procedure, and students have nothing to adjust against.




Tail trim
Tail trim is manual: bend and twist the tail by hand. Bending sets pitch, twisting sets roll. Work in small increments and expect to go back and forth - there is no scale and no reference mark, so the logged runs are the only feedback available.

title: Module 11 — Wet testing
text:
Cost of transport
Cost of transport is the score in Module 12, so measure it the same way every time:
\[\mathrm{COT} = \frac{P}{m \, g \, v} \tag{1}\]
with \(P\) the average electrical power over the run, \(m\) the robot’s mass, and \(v\) its average forward speed. It is dimensionless, and lower is better.
The two halves come from two different places:

Power, onboard. From the logged consumption above, averaged over the steady part of the run — not the acceleration at the start.
Speed, from the ceiling cameras. The overhead tracking in Figure 1 gives position against time, which is the honest way to get \(v\); timing it by eye across the tank is not good enough for a scored number.

Take both from the same window of the same run. Averaging power over one interval and speed over another is the most common way this number comes out wrong.






ImportantTBC



Still missing from the protocol:

Run profile — depth, duration, and the flap-frequency sweep to cover
Abort procedure — what conditions end a run early, and what the student does at the tank edge when they do
Camera tracking, practically — how a team starts a capture, and in what form the position data comes back









NoteCheckpoint



A completed underwater run with power, IMU and flapping frequency logged and successfully retrieved over BLE, no water ingress on inspection afterwards, and a cost-of-transport figure computed from Equation 1 with the camera-derived speed.
